metadata.title: How Does Claude Fill In a Financial Model?
metadata.purpose: Answer whether Claude fills in a 3-statement financial model by reasoning like an analyst, or by following a written set of steps that link an existing template. Lands the carry-out that a filled-in model is the numbers you gave it, linked by a fixed procedure -- not Claude's financial judgment.
metadata.source_note: Unlike some sibling redos, the source sheet's narration carries real skill-specific facts (not unfilled template placeholders) -- see QUESTION.md. Facts preserved: the 3-statement-model skill completes, populates, and links IS/BS/CF templates; Claude reads SKILL.md and executes steps linearly. Register re-registered Teardown -> Plain; source's B03 design-tell verdict became a plain mechanism + both-directions beat; a wrong-guess beat and an anchor (net income: IS -> retained earnings -> CF) were added per hai-simple's Phase 1 structure, since the source's Teardown shape carried neither.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (net income: income statement -> retained earnings -> cash flow statement)

beats.narration_text: People ask if Claude fills in a financial model by reasoning like an analyst. It doesn't. Liam here, in for Bear — let's take the skill apart and see what actually fills that model.

beats.narration_text: Here's the intuitive guess. Claude weighs your business the way an analyst would — pulling from general financial knowledge to decide what belongs where. The skill doesn't work that way. It's a fixed list of steps, written in advance, and Claude executes them linearly. Ask for something those steps don't cover and it won't improvise — it stays exactly inside what's written. They optimized for reproducibility at the expense of judgment. Same inputs, same procedure, same output — every time. That is the trade.

shot.new_visual_element: An analyst figure weighing judgment calls, struck through; a written checklist of steps lit instead

production_viz.label: Judgment, struck -- steps, lit
production_viz.mechanic: Left: a figure icon labelled 'ANALYST JUDGMENT' beside a thought-bubble of scattered decision marks. Right: a numbered checklist card labelled 'WRITTEN STEPS'. The analyst side dims and gets a terracotta strike; the checklist side stays lit. A final numbered step reads 'not on the list' and the analyst figure does not reach for it.

beats.narration_text: So here's the actual machinery. The skill reads a template that already lays out the three statements, and its whole job is to wire them together. Watch the anchor. Net income leaves the income statement, lands inside retained earnings on the balance sheet, and shows up again at the top of the cash flow statement. One number, three destinations, wired by a fixed procedure. Nothing is being reasoned about here. It's being connected.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- net income traveling from the income statement, through retained earnings on the balance sheet, into the cash flow statement

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- one number, three statements
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Three stacked cards labelled 'INCOME STATEMENT', 'BALANCE SHEET', 'CASH FLOW STATEMENT'. A single highlighted token 'NET INCOME' starts inside the income statement card, travels down into a highlighted row 'retained earnings' inside the balance sheet card, then travels again into a highlighted top row inside the cash flow card. Every other row on all three cards stays dim. THIS EXACT COMPOSITION RETURNS, FILLED IN, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: The link is built. The three statements tie together and the numbers land where they're supposed to. But here's the honest limit. Tying out is not the same as being right. The connections stay consistent even when the assumption feeding them is wrong — the procedure has no opinion about your input. And a blank line is not a broken run. It usually means the template's step for that line never got a number to connect. Tied out proves the wiring works. It doesn't prove the model is true.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS, tied together, then splits into 'tied out is not right' and 'blank is not broken'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- tied, then split
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 THREE-CARD COMPOSITION RETURNS, identical placement, now fully connected by a single unbroken line IS -> BS -> CF, all three cards lit. It shrinks and slides up. Two cards fade in beneath: left reads 'TIES OUT' with a checkmark, then a struck-through 'RIGHT' beneath it, labelled 'tied out is not right'; right reads 'LINE: BLANK' beside a faint 'no input given' note, labelled 'blank is not broken'.

beats.narration_text: A filled-in model isn't Claude's financial judgment. It's the numbers you gave it, wired by a fixed procedure. The template decides what connects — Claude just pulls the wires.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Hand it three plain assumptions — one revenue line, one expense, a starting cash balance — and ask it to run the three-statement model skill, then walk you through where each number lands on the income statement, the balance sheet, and the cash flow. Change one assumption and watch which lines move and which stay put. That's how you see the wiring instead of trusting it. Go deeper: ask it to describe a set of assumptions where the model would still tie out and still be flat wrong — and explain why the tie-out check misses it. Liam, in for Bear.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to see how a linked 3-statement model actually works. Here are three assumptions: year-one revenue = $500,000, year-one operating expense = $300,000, starting cash balance = $100,000. Walk me through building a 3-statement model with these inputs. Then, one line at a time, show me where each number lands on the income statement, the balance sheet, and the cash flow statement — and trace the anchor: net income leaving the income statement, being added to retained earnings on the balance sheet, and reappearing at the top of the cash flow statement. After that, change revenue to $800,000 and tell me exactly which lines on all three statements move, which stay the same, and how the model still ties out.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: describe a set of assumptions where the model would still tie out but be flat wrong — and explain why the tie-out check misses it.
